paras: The threat to burn the Allen home in Hope, Arkansas, was a warning delivered in early March 1919 by crowds of white residents to the family of Mrs. Jennie Allen, a Black woman whose French sister-in-law had come to stay with them. The visitor moved to a hotel on the advice of a local official, and no violence was reported. Several Black newspapers carried the story as an example of how Black soldiers and their French wives were treated on their return from the war.

Mrs. Mignon Avington, born Mignon Poste, had lived in a French town printed as "Savernay" and married Walter Avington, a Black American soldier, during the American occupation there. On her husband's advice she traveled to Hope to visit his sister, Mrs. Jennie Allen, while he remained in New York.

According to a Continental Press dispatch, "white citizens of this city threw a fit" when Mrs. Avington stepped off a train and asked to be taken to the Allen home, where a jitney brought her. Early that evening crowds collected at the station, described by the St. Louis Argus as "Arkansas 'crackers'," and sent word to the Allens that the house would be "burned to ashes" if she remained overnight. She said she would stay despite the threats, but George Atkins, identified as white and as chairman of the Council of Defense, advised her to spend the night at the Barlow Hotel. She left the Allen home "reluctantly" and spent the night at the hotel.

After about three days Mrs. Avington returned to New York, and the couple were said to be planning to go back to France. Speaking through an interpreter, she praised the record of Black troops in France and spoke of "America's contemptible customs in dealing with our people." No report of arrests or an investigation appears in the coverage.

The story reached the Black press as a Continental Press dispatch, and the Colorado Statesman ran it on March 15 under the headline "Town Objects to French Girl's Visit. Color Line Is Crashed; Soreheads Grumble for Hours." The Cleveland Gazette printed it the same day under "American Democracy," after a passage arguing that the army meant to push out Black officers and that returning Black soldiers would "not submit to American caste." The Philadelphia Tribune ran a shorter version, datelined March 10, among its Atglen, Pennsylvania, notes.

On March 21 the Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the Gazette's text under "Southerners Could Not Stand for," and the St. Louis Argus carried an uncredited copy that called the husband "Lieut. Walter Avington." All of the known versions trace to the single dispatch, and no account from an Arkansas paper appears in the coverage.

The datelines differ, reading March 7 in the Colorado Statesman, March 10 in the Philadelphia Tribune and March 21 in the St. Louis Argus, while the Gazette and Argus say only that she arrived "last week."

bases: Crowds at the station sent word to a Black family that their house would be burned if a French visitor stayed the night, and she left; no violence was carried out (A2, A5).
Every account is a version of one Continental Press dispatch (A2), reprinted or condensed in A1, A3, A4 and A5 with near-identical wording; no independent or local report was found.

accounts.label: Continental Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Crowds of white residents gathered at the station and warned the Allens their house would be burned if the French visitor stayed the night; on a white official's advice she moved to a hotel.

accounts.label: Philadelphia Tribune condensation
accounts.gist: A shorter version, datelined March 10, saying white people made sure she would not stay overnight with Avington's relatives; she spent the night at a hotel and returned to New York.

framing.detail: The Colorado Statesman headlined it 'Town Objects to French Girl's Visit. Color Line Is Crashed; Soreheads Grumble for Hours' and said white citizens 'threw a fit'.
The Cleveland Gazette placed it under 'American Democracy' beside a passage on the army's treatment of Black officers, as showing the 'French Wife of a Brave Afro-American Soldier'.
The Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the Gazette text under 'Southerners Could Not Stand for', after an item on passports denied to Black leaders.

versions.value: Dateline Hope, Ark., March 21 (a publication date for a story about 'last week')

conflicts.note: The datelines belong to the dispatch and its reprints, not to the threat itself; A1 and A5 place her arrival 'last week'. The Continental Press dateline of March 7 is the earliest.
Only the St. Louis Argus gives him an officer's rank.

Mrs. Mignon Avington and the household of Mrs. Jennie Allen.

info: The visit occurred in early March 1919, 'last week' before the March 15 issues; the dispatch is datelined Hope, March 7 (A2), March 10 (A3) and March 21 (A5); no exact date of the threat is given.
Hope, Arkansas: the railroad station, where crowds gathered, and the home of Mrs. Jennie Allen.
Mrs. Mignon (also printed 'Minion') Avington, a French woman married to Black soldier Walter Avington, and the household of his sister, Mrs. Jennie Allen, whose house was threatened.
None; the stated objection was that the French wife of a Black soldier would stay overnight with his family.
'White citizens of this city'; 'crowds' (A2), 'crowds of Arkansas "crackers"' (A5) who collected at the station.
She left the Allen home 'reluctantly', spent the night at the hotel, and after about three days returned to New York, where her husband was.

sources.note: Full story under 'American Democracy', framed by the treatment of Black soldiers; heavily garbled OCR; crowds of 'trackers' [crackers] threatened to burn the house.
